title: Master Comparison Table
note: Sorted fastest to slowest. "Order of Magnitude" is the typical access time rounded to a power of ten for quick comparison.

devices.name: CPU register
devices.dominantDelay: Electrical switching inside the CPU core

cost.text: Not sold separately (part of CPU die)

capacity.text: A few hundred bytes per core

facts: On the order of tens of picoseconds, effectively the same clock cycle as the instruction using them (Massachusetts Institute of Technology, n.d.)

devices.name: L1 cache
facts: About 1 nanosecond (roughly 4 CPU cycles) (ScienceDirect Topics, n.d.)

devices.name: L2 cache
devices.dominantDelay: On-die SRAM switching, one step further from the core
facts: About 3 nanoseconds (roughly 12 cycles) (ScienceDirect Topics, n.d.)

devices.name: L3 cache
devices.dominantDelay: Shared on-die SRAM, longer wire distance
facts: About 12 nanoseconds (roughly 26 cycles on average) (ScienceDirect Topics, n.d.)

devices.name: DRAM (main memory)
devices.dominantDelay: Row activation and charge sensing in the memory cell
devices.typicalUse: Running programs and their working data
facts: Roughly 30 to 100 nanoseconds per random access, ten to a hundred times slower than L1 cache (ScienceDirect Topics, n.d.)

devices.name: Byte-addressable NVM (e.g., Intel Optane)
devices.accessText: Between DRAM and NAND flash (no single published figure)
devices.dominantDelay: Phase-change/resistive cell access, no block erase needed

capacity.text: Up to a few hundred GB per module

devices.typicalUse: Persistent memory tier, cache for slower SSDs
devices.source: Product discontinued by Intel in 2022. Qualitative positioning only
facts: Intel Optane is described only by its position in the hierarchy and its 2022 discontinuation, not by an invented precise latency number, because no source in the allowed list (textbooks, vendor datasheets, standards bodies, .edu notes) published one during this research pass.

devices.name: Raw NAND flash cell (component level)
devices.typicalUse: Building block inside all flash-based storage
facts: At the raw NAND chip level, a page read takes on the order of 10 microseconds, roughly a thousand times faster than the HDD figures (University of Washington, 2023)

devices.name: NVMe SSD
devices.dominantDelay: NAND chip read plus a lightweight PCIe/NVMe protocol

capacity.text: 500 GB to 4+ TB (consumer), up to tens of TB (enterprise)

devices.source: University of Washington, 2023 / NVM Express, n.d. / Samsung Electronics, 2023
facts: NVMe SSDs use a streamlined protocol built for flash, already demonstrated past 1,000,000 IOPS, with up to 64,000 queues of 64,000 commands each (NVM Express, n.d.)
A current NVMe drive is rated for sequential reads around 7,450 MB/s (Samsung Electronics, 2023), well beyond what the SATA interface itself can carry

devices.name: SATA SSD
devices.accessText: Tens to a few hundred microseconds, host-visible
devices.calloutText: tens to a few hundred µs
devices.dominantDelay: Same NAND chip plus the older, heavier AHCI/SATA protocol
devices.source: NVM Express, n.d. / University of Washington, 2023
facts: SATA SSDs use the older AHCI protocol, capped at about 200,000 IOPS with one queue of 32 commands (NVM Express, n.d.)

devices.name: USB flash drive / SD card
devices.accessText: Similar order to SSD flash, often slower in practice
devices.dominantDelay: NAND cell plus a simpler controller and USB/SD bus overhead
facts: USB flash drives and SD/microSD cards use the same NAND flash principle as SSDs, but usually with simpler, cheaper controllers and a slower bus, so real-world access is slower than an internal SSD even though the underlying memory is similar (Kingston Technology, n.d.)

devices.name: HDD, 15,000 RPM (enterprise)
devices.accessText: ~2.0 ms rotational + seek, roughly 5 to 6 ms total

capacity.text: Hundreds of GB to a few TB

facts: 15,000 RPM is about 2.0 ms average rotational latency as rated by the manufacturer (Seagate Technology, 2015)

devices.name: HDD, 7,200 RPM (desktop/enterprise)
devices.accessText: ~4.16 ms rotational + seek, roughly 9 to 13 ms total
facts: 7,200 RPM is about 4.16 ms average rotational latency as measured on a real drive (Seagate Technology, 2019)
Average seek time on desktop-class drives: about 3 to 12 ms, 9 ms is a commonly cited typical figure (Weiss, n.d.)

devices.name: HDD, 5,400 RPM (laptop/consumer)
devices.accessText: ~5.6 ms rotational + seek, roughly 15 to 16 ms total
devices.dominantDelay: Rotational latency and seek together, slower spindle
facts: Worked figure, calculated from the formula rather than the lesson slides: 5,400 RPM is about 5.6 ms average rotational latency (average latency = half of one full rotation, rotation time = 60 / RPM) (Weiss, n.d.) (Stanford University, n.d.)
Total average access time runs to about 15 to 16 ms on a slow 5,400 RPM drive (Weiss, n.d.) (Stanford University, n.d.)

devices.name: Network / cloud storage (round trip)
devices.accessText: ~8 ms (same metro area) to 270+ ms (opposite side of the world)
devices.dominantDelay: Physical distance and number of network hops, not the storage device itself

cost.text: Pay-per-use, no fixed per-GB hardware cost

facts: A round trip to a nearby data center runs about 8 ms, while a round trip to a data center on the other side of the world can run past 270 ms (Microsoft Corporation, 2026)

devices.name: Optical disc (CD/DVD/Blu-ray)
devices.accessText: Roughly 100 to 300 ms (estimated order of magnitude, no single vendor spec found)
devices.dominantDelay: Laser must jump across a spiral track, not concentric rings
devices.source: Order-of-magnitude estimate, no exact vendor figure located
facts: Drive makers publish read speed ("16x") rather than one access-time number. Published academic material puts it roughly two orders of magnitude behind a hard disk

No vendor datasheet located during research publishes a single official "access time" figure for CD/DVD/Blu-ray drives. The figure is an order-of-magnitude range drawn from academic course material, flagged as an estimate rather than a hard spec.

devices.name: Magnetic tape (LTO-9), locating one file
devices.accessText: 10 to 100 seconds to locate, plus 4-10 s robotic mount and ~11 s drive load
devices.dominantDelay: Physically winding the tape to the right position

capacity.text: 18 TB native, 45 TB compressed per cartridge

facts: Native transfer rate is 400 MB/s, 1,000 MB/s compressed (LTO Program, n.d.)
Finding one specific file means a robotic mount (4 to 10 seconds), a drive load (about 11 seconds), and then locating the file on the tape (10 to 100 seconds) (Moore, 2020)
Once the tape is positioned, it streams data faster than most hard disks (360 to 400 MB/s vs. 160 to 220 MB/s) (Moore, 2020)
